title: Integrations
markdown:
External channels connect callers to the Executive. Each inbound adapter resolves the sender to a Person via `find_person_by_{slack,discord,telegram,email}_id` and threads `person_id` into `Executive.chat()`.

### Inbound channels

- **Slack** (`integrations.slack_bot`) — async Bolt socket-mode (`AsyncApp` + `AsyncSocketModeHandler`) embedded in the lifespan; responds to `@mention`s, DMs, and thread continuations, with per-conversation session memory (see **Conversation state** below). Text only: there is no interactivity endpoint and no Block Kit, so nothing Slack sends carries a button.
- **Discord** (`integrations.discord_bot`) — discord.py gateway embedded in the lifespan; per-thread auto-titling, session-scoped memory, author attribution, configurable `@mention` thread promotion.
- **Telegram** — webhook gating + per-chat history.
- **Google Chat** — webhook + service-account auth. It resolves no approval gates and has no roster gate (the webhook authenticates Google, not the sender), and it never populates the session's trusted alert ids, so `ack_alert`'s trust check — which now runs on every session rather than only those declaring an `origin_channel` — refuses there by default, and its `<channel>` block says plainly that a sign-off cannot be answered from it.
- **Email** (`integrations.email_poller`) — IMAP poll loop; strips Reply-To, filters auto-replies. The Executive sees the whole message; peer memory records only `_email_memory_text` — the subject, the sender's new text (cut at the first quoted or forwarded message) and the attachment filenames — parsed without backtracking-prone regexes, since the text is sender-controlled, and only for a rostered sender, the only kind with a peer to record into.

Slack, Discord, and Telegram are roster-gated on inbound: an unrostered sender's message is silently dropped (`details.outcome="rejected_unknown_sender"`). Email is not inbound-gated — non-roster mail flows through with a `[POLICY]` notice so triage can classify it. Slack/Discord thread continuations pass the shared `integrations.response_gate` (utility-fast model, biased toward replying).

### Conversation state

Every adapter keys a deterministic `session_id` off the conversation surface and replays that session's stored turns into `Session.conversation_history`, so a follow-up ("yes, go ahead") lands with the question still in context. Slack's ids are `slack:dm:{user}`, `slack:thread:{channel}:{thread_ts}`, and `slack:channel:{channel}:{user}` for a mention that starts a thread; because the bot's reply roots a Slack thread at that message's `ts`, the turn is double-written to that thread's session too, so the first continuation inside it is not cold. A reply inside a thread THAT PERSON ROOTED also offers the parent `slack:channel:{channel}:{user}` id when matching an approval gate, since a gate raised on the mention recorded that session while the answer arrives under the thread's. The root-author check is load-bearing: widening on "threaded and not a DM" alone offered one person's channel session inside any thread in that channel, so a remark they made to a colleague could resolve their open gate and post the run's title into that colleague's thread. Discord has the same shape — its auto-thread router promotes a mention reply into a bot-owned thread — and the same alias. An @-mention inside a DM is handled once, by the DM path: Slack fires both events, and taking both forked the conversation across two session ids. The same id is the audit grouping key and the scope passed to `format_for_prompt`. A per-session `asyncio.Lock` serializes turns within one conversation — the inflight semaphore caps fan-out across the workspace, which does nothing to stop two messages in the same thread from both reading history before either writes it. Persistence happens after the reply is sent and its failure is logged, never surfaced: the user already has their answer.

This was absent on Slack until #136. Every message built a fresh `Session` and minted a per-*message* id (`thread_ts` falls back to the message's own `ts`, so a DM never repeated one), which meant a multi-turn confirmation could not work: the Executive asked whether to send a briefing to Slack, the user said yes, and the next turn had no record of the question.

### What the model is told about the channel

Chat adapters pass a `<channel>` block (`integrations.channel_context`) in the **user turn** — never a cached system block. It names the surface, states that the person cannot see the app's cards or buttons, and draws the line the assistant kept crossing: briefing proposals and alerts are actioned on the briefing page; a proposal that books something can only be approved there; a workflow sign-off the Executive is explicitly waiting on *can* be answered in the conversation. The principal's DMs on Slack, Discord and Telegram also receive the open-alert digest (`briefing.context.format_open_alerts_for_prompt`) as the `<briefing>` block, gated to DMs because the board is company-wide and a shared channel must not pull it in. That digest is the ONLY trusted source of an `alert_id` for `ack_alert`. The briefing page's `[Discuss mode — alert_id=N]` primer is a pointer to which item is under discussion, not authority on its own: the server accepts that id only if it is also on the live board it derived itself. An id appearing anywhere else, including inside an alert's own body, is not trusted: alerts are minted from inbound email and chat, so their bodies are attacker-controlled. Two mechanisms enforce that rather than one prompt rule. Every field the digest interpolates is collapsed to a single line, because a newline in an attacker-written headline, suggested action, tag or review note would otherwise forge a whole extra `[N]` line — a fabricated instruction to clear somebody else's alert. And the live board the server derived is recorded on the session, so `ack_alert` refuses any id outside it — on EVERY session, web included; the web previously had no check at all. The recorded set is the whole live board (the cap `/today` renders as cards), not just the rows the digest printed, so a card past the digest's 30-row render cap is still ackable rather than sending the principal back to the page. Be precise about what this buys: it stops an id that is invented, closed, snoozed or expired, including one quoted out of an attacker-written alert body. It does NOT stop the model being argued into acking the wrong LIVE card — one alert's body can still make a case about another id that is genuinely open. Scoping trust to the single item under discussion would need the primer id carried server-side, which it is not.

### Handler failures

An adapter's catch-all replies "I encountered an error processing your request." On Slack that used to be the whole story — one uncorrelated log line, no audit row, and an unguarded error-send that could itself escape into Bolt. It now logs with the session, sender, channel, thread and mode, and writes an `integration_inbound` row with `details.outcome="handler_error"`, joining the inbound row under the same `session_id`. Upstream, a single crashing tool handler no longer takes the turn down at all: the orchestrator's tool gathers use `return_exceptions=True`, hand the model an error `tool_result`, and audit it with `ok=false` (cancellation is re-raised, not swallowed).

### Attachments

`integrations.attachments` handles web chat, Discord, and Telegram. Images become Anthropic vision blocks; documents (PDF/DOCX/TXT/MD/CSV) are inlined into the turn that carried them and indexed into the ChromaDB `inbound_attachments` collection. 20 MB/file cap; web chat uses `POST /chat/upload`.

Indexed chunks are keyed on `attachment:<bare filename>` and tagged `type=attachment`. An attachment's name is chosen by whoever sent the message and the name is the chunk-id namespace, so without the prefix an inbound `strategy-2026.md` would upsert over the curated company document of that name. The prefix separates inbound content from curated uploads and keeps provenance visible; it does not separate senders from one another.

Isolation is the **collection**: `retriever.retrieve` never queries `inbound_attachments` at all, so an attachment cannot resurface as company knowledge in a later, unrelated turn. Attachment processing is roster-gated on Discord too — it previously ran before the gate, so an unrostered sender's file was downloaded and indexed before their message was dropped. These rows still have no operator surface: they are never written to `company/docs/`, so `GET /documents` does not list them.

This replaced a domain-based scheme that did not work. The chunks lived in `company_docs` under a domain outside the specialist set, on the premise that an unrecognised domain matched no filter. It matched every one — `ChromaDBStore.query` attaches a `where` clause only when a domain filter is present, and an Executive-level retrieval passes none — so attachments came back under “From your company documents”, top-ranked and indistinguishable from a curated upload. Legacy rows are migrated across on boot.

### MCP gateway & outbound

MCP runs in **both directions**. As a *client*, `orchestrator.mcp_gateway.MCPGateway` proxies MCP servers (Gmail, Calendar, Drive — whatever `mcp_servers.json` configures) as Executive tools, with egress gating on Gmail recipients, Calendar attendees, and Drive share grantees against the roster (and a refusal of public / whole-domain Drive sharing). The Google Workspace server (`workspace-mcp`) behind those Gmail/Calendar/Drive tools runs **co-located inside the API** as a stdio child of the gateway — fitting the single-tenant model (one install = one company = one exec Google account), so there's no separate service to operate. It's baked into the API image and launched by `docker/workspace-mcp-launch.sh`, which selects single-user OAuth (token persisted at `/data/google_credentials`) or service-account domain-wide delegation from `GWORKSPACE_AUTH_MODE`. The gateway forwards the Google secrets to the child via `_FORWARDED_ENV_VARS`. As a *server*, `openexecutive.mcp_server` exposes OE's own company context and specialist council to external MCP clients at `/mcp` — the inverse direction; see the dedicated **MCP Server** section. The gateway launches extensible-mcp as a `uvx` subprocess whose fastembed tool-search index uses an embedding model baked into the API image and loaded offline, so it no longer re-downloads that model from the Hugging Face Hub on every cold start. extensible-mcp is pinned twice over: to a commit, which fixes its own code, and with `--exclude-newer`, which fixes the resolution of its dependencies — without the cutoff uvx re-resolves them against PyPI on every networked start, so a new release of any of them would reach running deployments on restart. Both live in `_EXTENSIBLE_MCP_LAUNCH_ARGS` in `orchestrator/mcp_gateway.py`, the Dockerfile's pre-warm uses the same arguments (a unit test enforces the match), so an image whose pre-warm succeeded starts the gateway with no network. The pre-warm is best-effort (`|| true`): an image built while GitHub was unreachable fetches the pinned commit on its first start instead. Updating the gateway is a deliberate bump of the commit and cutoff; `uv` itself is not pinned. Because the MCP stdio client does not inherit the parent environment, `MCPGateway.start()` explicitly forwards the embedding-cache/offline env vars (`FASTEMBED_CACHE_PATH`, `HF_HUB_OFFLINE`, …) into the child.

**Enablement, and why it degrades instead of dying.** `MCP_ENABLED` left unset is inferred from the presence of `mcp_servers_config_path` — dropping an `mcp_servers.json` next to `profile.yaml` turns MCP on with no further configuration. An **explicit** setting always wins in both directions: `MCP_ENABLED=false` keeps MCP off with the file still in place. It did not: `_resolve_mcp` tested `not self.mcp_enabled`, which cannot tell "never set" from "set to false", so the file's presence silently overrode the operator. The file is probed through `config.mcp_config_file_present`, never `Path.exists` directly — that re-raises an EACCES on a parent directory, and from inside a validator that comes out of `Settings()` itself, which `api/main.py` calls at module level. The check now reads `model_fields_set` (the fields the env actually supplied) and stores that on a private attr behind the read-only `mcp_auto_enabled` property, because the validator's own assignment joins that set and would otherwise make every auto-enable look explicit downstream.

Startup is **best-effort**, in `main._start_mcp_gateway`. Two checks come before the subprocess: MCP off is a no-op, and a config defining no servers under `mcpServers` is logged and skipped — extensible-mcp's own loader raises on that and exits, and because the child is already gone the only thing that surfaces is anyio's "Attempted to exit cancel scope in a different task" from `stdio_client` unwinding, a traceback naming nothing about configuration. The start is also bounded (120s, generous because that child may still clone extensible-mcp on a cold start if the image's pre-warm failed): `ClientSession` carries no `read_timeout_seconds`, so `initialize()` waits forever on a child that is *alive but silent*, and an unbounded wait is a lifespan that never yields — the same healthcheck-never-passes symptom, which no `except` can see. A gateway that fails anyway is logged at ERROR with the config path, the servers it named, and whether the config file or an explicit `MCP_ENABLED` turned MCP on, then torn down under its own timeout; the API boots **without MCP tools and without the email poller** rather than refusing to boot. The guard catches `BaseException`, not `Exception`, re-raising a bare `CancelledError` first: the original failure came from anyio, which wraps a task group's failures in `BaseExceptionGroup` as soon as one is a `BaseException` — and that group is not an `Exception`, so `except Exception` would miss the very shape this contains. The teardown is contained too, since it runs from inside that `except` and would otherwise replace the actionable log with the crash it prevents. `configured_server_names` never raises either, and deliberately catches broadly: it reads an operator-owned path during startup, where an exception is the crash loop rather than a bug report — `Path.is_file` re-raises an EACCES on a parent directory, and `json.loads` answers deeply-nested input with `RecursionError`, which is not a `ValueError`. It tests `is_file()` so a directory or a symlink to a FIFO is never opened, and caps the read at 1 MiB. That exception used to propagate out of the lifespan and kill the container — under `restart: unless-stopped`, a crash loop whose only outward symptom was a healthcheck that never passed. Outbound tools: per-Person DMs (`send_slack_dm`, `send_discord_dm`, `send_telegram_message`) plus room-targeted `send_department_message` and `send_company_broadcast`. The per-Person DMs are additionally rate-limited and de-duplicated by the outbound anti-spam guard (below).

### Outbound anti-spam guard

Every per-Person DM passes a deterministic guard (`orchestrator.outbound_guard.check_outbound_allowed`) after the roster gate and recipient-id recovery but before the network send — the single chokepoint **all** proactive DM paths reach (ad-hoc chat sends, the scheduler's followup/nudge dispatch, principal-brief delivery, the reflection turn, and research-finding routing). On a violation it returns a human-readable reason and the handler **suppresses** the send (`{"status":"suppressed","reason":…}`), writes a `tool_invocation` audit row with `suppressed=true`, and writes **no** `done` activity row — so a blocked attempt never counts toward its own rate cap, and the Executive can read the reason and hold or `schedule_followup` for the recipient's next window. Three controls: **content dedup** (a near-identical message — whitespace/case-normalized, first 160 chars — already sent to the same recipient within `OUTBOUND_DEDUP_WINDOW_MINUTES`, default 360); a **per-recipient rate cap** (`OUTBOUND_MAX_PER_RECIPIENT_PER_WINDOW`, default 5, over `OUTBOUND_RATE_WINDOW_MINUTES`, default 60); and **quiet hours / availability** (`OUTBOUND_RESPECT_QUIET_HOURS`, default on — refuse while the recipient is on leave or outside their `people.channel` availability windows, surfacing the next open window). Delivery history is read from the existing `status='done'` `scheduled_actions` rows (`episodic.recent_sends_for_channel_ref`), so there is no new table. The guard is **fail-open**: any internal lookup error returns "allow", so it can never turn a working send into a crash or a silently-dropped message. Principal briefs and the internal heartbeat kinds use the `__internal__` channel and never reach these handlers, so they are unaffected.

### Calendar & Google Meet

The Executive books meetings through two typed tools over the Calendar MCP. `create_calendar_event` schedules a **future** meeting (propose→approve by default, or auto-execute once that decision class is promoted) and may be used proactively when a stalled goal warrants a sync. `create_instant_meeting` spins up an **impromptu call starting now**, auto-executing without the approval step and skipping the business-hours/horizon caps, so the Executive can hand back a join link immediately. Both attach a **Google Meet** link by default (`add_google_meet`; opt out for in-person), parsed from the created event's `conferenceData` and surfaced to the caller plus persisted on the decision ledger. Either way the caps that matter still hold — roster membership, principal-protection, max attendees, and a daily booking ceiling.

**Around-the-meeting participation.** The Executive doesn't join the call as a live voice; instead, on every successful booking it schedules a best-effort post-meeting follow-up (~5 min after the end) that DMs a human attendee asking for a quick recap — key decisions and action items. The reply flows back through the same cross-session DM context linkage described below, so the Executive can act on it (summarize, follow up) in a later turn. No meeting-transcript or Drive integration is required.

### Cross-session DM context

When the principal says "DM Alex about X" in one session, OE sends the DM and — if a live conversation is active — records an `outbound_context` linkage row (recipient, full outbound text, originating session id). Email is covered too but recorded one layer deeper — there is no `send_email` tool, so the linkage is written in `orchestrator.mcp_gateway` after a successful `google_workspace__send_gmail_message`, one row per `to`/`cc` recipient keyed by the bare lowercased address (OE's own address skipped). When Alex later replies on the 1:1 DM path — or by email — the shared helper `integrations.inbound_hydration.hydrate_user_message` (called by the Discord, Telegram, and Slack handlers, and by the email poller keyed on the sender address) looks up the most-recent `open` linkage for that sender within 72h and prepends an `<outbound_reply_context>` block — the outbound text plus a backstory excerpt from the originating session — to the message handed to `Executive.chat()`. So OE knows what the reply is about instead of starting from an empty per-person session. The block is context for the LLM turn only: peer memory strips it before recording what the person said (`strip_outbound_reply_context`, applied in `sync_turn`, `sync_department_turn` and to the prefetch query), so the Executive's own DM is never attributed to the person who replied to it. The block lands in the user turn (caching rule) and is injected into a copy only — the pristine reply is persisted to history. The linkage is one-shot (consumed on first matched reply, race-safe) so an unrelated later DM isn't re-hydrated. This is deterministic and independent of the per-person `peer_memory` (Honcho) layer.

Every adapter that persists a turn (Slack, Discord, Telegram, and the web route) records the message's **resolved sender** on `chat_messages.sender_person_id` — the rostered Person the adapter matched, or NULL for an unrostered sender — independently of the session owner, which falls back to the principal on Discord and Telegram so those threads stay visible. Attunement's open loops and feedback rely on this so an outsider's words are never read as someone on the roster's.
